title: Fast input and output
objectives: Read and write large inputs quickly in Python and C++.

screens.title: Two ways to read
screens.prose: Both programs read $n = 2 \cdot 10^5$ numbers, one per line, and build the same list. On Codeforces, reading alone can decide between Accepted and Time limit exceeded.

lines: # A: one line at a time
params.title: Reading 200,000 numbers

screens.question: Which reads faster, and roughly by how much?

options.text: B, several times faster
A: it reads only what it needs
options.why: You judged by the memory used. Each `input()` call has a fixed cost, paid $2 \cdot 10^5$ times.

options.text: The same: both read the same bytes
options.why: The bytes are the same, but A makes $2 \cdot 10^5$ calls and B makes one.

hints.text: Count the calls each program makes.
Line 3 calls `input()` once per number.
B reads once and splits once; A pays the cost of a call $2 \cdot 10^5$ times.

feedback.correct: One read and one split beat $2 \cdot 10^5$ separate calls.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the calls, not the bytes.

byKey.a: You chose A. Each `input()` call costs time on its own, $2 \cdot 10^5$ times over.
byKey.same: Same bytes, but A makes $2 \cdot 10^5$ calls and B one.

explain.text: Measured in CPython in this sandbox, A took about 0.14 s and B about 0.04 s. In this app's Pyodide, A took about 0.19 s and B 0.06 s. Several such costs add up, and a slow judge machine multiplies them.

screens.title: Fast input and output
screens.prose: This is **fast input**: read everything at once, split it into tokens, and walk them with a position. **Fast output** is its mirror: collect the answers and print them once.
screens.question: Put the steps of a fast program in order.

lines.text: For each test case: `n = int(data[pos])`, take the next `n` tokens, move `pos` on
Append the test case's answer to a list `out`

hints.text: Nothing can be split before it is read.
The first token is $t$.
Read and split, take $t$, loop over the test cases collecting answers, then print once.

feedback.correct: Read once, walk the tokens, print once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the data: read, take $t$, loop, collect, print.

explain.text: The program touches the input once and the output once, whatever $t$ is. Everything between is plain list work, which is fast.

screens.title: A grid of strings
screens.prose: A map of the trading floor: $h$ rows of $w$ characters, `#` for a desk. After `data = text.split()`, each row is one token, since a row has no spaces.

params.title: Input: h w, then h rows

screens.question: Which expression is row $r$ of the grid, counting rows from 0?

options.text: `data[2 + r]`
`data[r]`
options.why: You forgot the two tokens for $h$ and $w$ before the rows.

options.text: `data[1 + r]`
options.why: You counted the first line as one token. `3 4` splits into two.

hints.text: Write out the tokens in order.
Line 1 holds two tokens.

feedback.correct: Two header tokens, then one token per row.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the tokens, starting with the two numbers on line 1.

byKey.one: You counted `3 4` as one token. `split()` makes it two.

explain.text: `split()` gives `['3', '4', '#..#', '.##.', '....']`, so row $r$ is `data[2 + r]`. With `sys.stdin.buffer` the tokens are bytes, such as `b'#..#'`. Test a character with `row[c] == ord('#')`, or decode the row first.

screens.title: Printing many lines
screens.prose: Output costs time too. Each version prints $10^5$ answers, one per line.
screens.question: Which is fastest?

options.text: 2: one string, one `print`
1: `print` is the simplest
options.why: You chose the simplest. `print` does extra work on every call, $10^5$ times.

options.text: 3: `write` skips `print`'s formatting
options.why: That helps, but it still makes $10^5$ calls. One `join` and one write is fewer.

hints.text: Count the calls each version makes.
Version 2 makes one call.
1 and 3 call once per line; 2 builds one string with `join` and prints it once.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count calls, as with input.

byKey.loop: You chose `print` in a loop: $10^5$ calls, each with its own overhead.

explain.text: Timed in CPython here for $10^5$ lines: loop 0.17 s, `write` 0.08 s, `join` 0.01 s. In this app's runner output goes to memory, so the gap is smaller. The rule is the same as for input: one call, not one per line.

screens.title: The same in C++
screens.prose: In C++ the two lines in the box make `std::cin` and `std::cout` fast. This program has them, but prints with `std::endl`. Timed with g++ here for $10^6$ numbers: 0.86 s with neither line, 0.12 s with both. Adding `std::endl` made it 0.54 s.
screens.question: Why does `std::endl` give back most of the gain?

options.text: It flushes the output after every line: $10^6$ writes to the system
It writes a longer line ending than `'\n'`
options.why: It writes the same newline. The cost is the flush that follows it.

options.text: It turns the stdio sync back on
options.why: It does not change the sync. It forces the buffer out, line after line.

hints.text: What does `std::endl` do besides end the line?
Line 5 runs once per number.
`std::endl` is `'\n'` plus a flush. Write `'\n'` and let the buffer fill.

feedback.correct: A flush per line; `'\n'` lets the buffer collect output.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. `std::endl` does two things, and one of them is slow.

byKey.newline: The newline is the same character. `std::endl` also flushes, and that is the cost.

explain.text: `sync_with_stdio(false)` stops C++ streams keeping in step with C's `stdio`, so they buffer on their own. `cin.tie(nullptr)` stops `cin` flushing `cout` before every read. `std::endl` then forces a flush per line, which undoes much of that.

screens.title: Values on two lines
screens.prose: This statement says: *the $n$ values of a test case are given on one or more lines*. The program reads each test case's values with one `input()`. Run it in your head on the input shown.
screens.question: What does the program print for test case 1?

options.why: That is the right answer, read as the statement means. The program reads one line, `4 1`, and stops there.

options.text: It crashes on line 3
options.why: Line 3 is a whole line of values; `split()` handles the space. The trouble comes later.

hints.text: What does one `input()` return?
Test case 1 has $n = 3$, but its values sit on lines 3 and 4.
`input()` returns `4 1`, so `a = [4, 1]` and the program prints `5 4`. Then it reads `5` as the next $n$.

feedback.correct: `5 4`: it read only line 3, then took `5` as the next $n$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow `input()` one line at a time.

byKey.right: You read the input as the statement means it. `input()` returns one line, `4 1`, so the program prints `5 4`.

explain.text: `input()` reads one line, so the program read `4 1` and missed the 5. It then took that 5 as test case 2's $n$ and printed `2 2`. Reading tokens with `split()` on the whole input cannot fall out of step like this.

screens.title: The fast template
screens.prose:
Read every token at once, walk them with a position, print once:

```python
import sys
data = sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()
t, pos, out = int(data[0]), 1, []
for _ in range(t):
    n = int(data[pos]); pos += 1
    a = list(map(int, data[pos:pos + n]))
    pos += n
    out.append(f"{sum(a)} {max(a)}")
print("\n".join(out))
```
screens.question: Why does this template survive the trap's input?

options.text: `split()` ignores line breaks, so values may sit on any line
It reads bytes, which keep the line breaks
options.why: Bytes or text, `split()` drops the line breaks. That is the point.

options.text: It is faster, so it reads more
options.why: Speed does not change what is read. Token order does.

feedback.correct: Tokens carry no line structure, so nothing can fall out of step.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what `split()` does with a line break.

explain.text: `split()` with no argument splits on any run of spaces, tabs and newlines. Blank lines, a missing final newline and values over several lines all give the same tokens.

screens.title: A token reader
screens.prose: Write `read_tokens(data)`. It takes the whole input as bytes and returns an **iterator** of ints. A program then calls `next(it)` for each number. `int(b'12')` is 12.
screens.question: Write `read_tokens(data)`.

tests.call: all(type(x) is int for x in read_tokens(b'1 22 333'))

tests.setup: data = b' '.join(str(i).encode() for i in range(200000))

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests: no final newline, Windows line endings, blank lines, tabs, an empty input, and 200,000 tokens. Tests 6 and 7 check that the result is an iterator, not a list.

hints.text: `data.split()` already gives the tokens as bytes.
`map(int, ...)` converts lazily and is an iterator.
`return map(int, data.split())`.

feedback.correct: One split, and `map` converts each token when it is asked for.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test.

byKey.test-6: Test 6 calls `next` on your result. A list is not an iterator; wrap it in `iter(...)` or use `map`.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 checks `iter(it) is it`, true only of an iterator. A list gives a new iterator each time.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 has Windows line endings, `\r\n`. `split()` with no argument removes them; `split(b'\n')` does not.

explain.text: `data.split()` splits on any whitespace, including `\r`, tabs and blank lines. `map(int, ...)` hands out one int per `next`, so a program never needs `pos` at all.

widget.solution:
import sys

data = sys.stdin.read().split()
t = int(data[0])
pos = 1
out = []
for _ in range(t):
    n = int(data[pos])
    pos += 1
    a = list(map(int, data[pos:pos + n]))
    pos += n
    out.append(f"{sum(a)} {max(a)}")
print("\n".join(out))
widget.how: Check runs your program 7 times, each with its own input, and compares what it prints. Test 4 has no final newline. Test 5 has blank lines and values over two lines, and test 7 has $t = 10^4$ test cases.

The values of one test case may sit on several lines.
Walk `pos` through the tokens, append `f"{sum(a)} {max(a)}"` for each test case, then print the joined list once.

feedback.correct: Read once, walk the tokens, print once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test's input.

byKey.test-5: Test 5 has a blank line and a test case whose values sit on two lines. Read tokens, not lines.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 has no newline at the end. Reading tokens handles that; reading lines may not.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 has $10^4$ test cases. Check that `pos` moves past every value.

explain.text: The program reads once and splits once, so blank lines and broken lines cannot confuse it. It prints once, so $10^4$ answers cost one call. Python's integers also hold test 6's sum of $5 \cdot 10^9$ without overflow.

Read `n`, then `n` values into a `long long` sum and maximum, and print with `'\n'`, not `std::endl`.

screens.title: Replays and interviews
screens.prose: Fast reading matters outside contests. Replaying a day of market data or scanning a log can mean $10^7$ lines, where reading is half the work. C++ developer interviews at trading firms ask about it directly.

lines: prices with std::cin and it is slow.
and it got several times faster. Why?
params.title: Interview

screens.question: What is the best answer?

options.text: C++ streams stop keeping in step with C's `stdio`, so `cin` can buffer its input on its own
It moves reading onto a second thread
options.why: You guessed at threads. The stream simply stops synchronising with `stdio` after every operation.

options.text: It turns off error checking in `>>`
options.why: Parsing and error checks still run. The saving is in buffering.

hints.text: What is being synchronised with what?
The name says it: sync with `stdio`.
By default `cin` stays in step with C's `scanf` buffer, which costs time on every read. Turning that off lets it buffer.

feedback.correct: No sync with `stdio`, so the stream buffers freely.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The line turns off a synchronisation, nothing more.

byKey.thread: You chose a thread. Nothing runs in parallel; the stream just buffers on its own.

explain.text: By default C++ streams stay in step with C's `stdio` so the two can be mixed. Turning that off lets `cin` read large blocks, which is the gain we measured. After it, do not mix `scanf` with `cin`.

ideas: Read the whole input at once and split it into tokens. Walk them with a position, or with `next` on an iterator.
Collect the answers and print them once with `"\n".join(...)`; in C++ use `sync_with_stdio(false)`, `cin.tie(nullptr)` and `'\n'`.
Tokens ignore line structure, so blank lines, a missing final newline and values over several lines cannot break the reader.

formula.name: The fast template
formula.note: Then `pos` walks the tokens and one `print` writes every answer.

summary.trap: `input().split()` reads one line; when values may span lines, it falls out of step with the input.

quiz.prose: A Python solution prints $10^5$ answers with `print(x)` inside its main loop and is too slow on the judge.
quiz.question: Which change helps most?

options.text: Collect the answers in a list and `print("\n".join(map(str, out)))` once
Add `flush=True` to each `print`
options.why: You added a flush to each call. That makes every line slower, not faster.

options.text: Format each answer with an f-string before printing
options.why: Formatting is not the cost. The $10^5$ separate calls are.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the calls to `print`.

explain.text: Each `print` call has overhead, paid $10^5$ times. Building one string with `join` and printing it once pays it once.

quiz.prose: A C++ solution prints $2 \cdot 10^5$ lines with `std::cout << ans << std::endl;`.
quiz.question: What is the cheapest fix?

options.text: Write `'\n'` instead of `std::endl`
Switch to `printf` but keep the same loop
options.why: That can work, but it is a bigger change. The cost is the flush in `std::endl`.

options.text: Store `ans` as `long long`
options.why: The type does not change the speed of printing. The flush does.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what `std::endl` does besides end the line.

explain.text: `std::endl` writes a newline and flushes the buffer, once per line. `'\n'` lets the buffer fill and go out in large blocks.

quiz.prose: The input text is `"2\n\n5 -3"`: a blank line in the middle and no final newline.
quiz.question: How many tokens does `text.split()` give?

feedback.correct: Three: the blank line and the missing newline make no difference.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. `split()` with no argument drops all whitespace.

byKey.blank: You counted the blank line as a token. `split()` with no argument drops it.
byKey.lines: You counted words on the first line only, or lines with text. Count every number.

explain.text: `split()` with no argument treats any run of whitespace as one break and ignores it at the ends. So the tokens are `2`, `5` and `-3`.

quiz.prose: On Codeforces you read with `data = sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()`. The input starts with `3`.
quiz.question: What is `data[0] == "3"`?

options.text: `False`: `data[0]` is the bytes `b'3'`
`True`: it is the first token
options.why: You treated the token as text. `buffer` gives bytes, and `b'3'` never equals `'3'`.

options.text: It raises an error
options.why: Comparing bytes with text is allowed in Python 3; it is simply `False`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what type `buffer.read()` returns.

explain.text: `sys.stdin.buffer` reads bytes, so every token is bytes. `int(data[0])` still works; comparisons with text need `b'3'` or `.decode()` first.
